entities.name: Grimms' fairy tales
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Grimms' Fairy Tales, a seminal collection of German folktales compiled and published by Wilhelm and Jacob Grimm between 1812 and 1857, encapsulates the essence of European folklore while significantly influencing the literary landscape. Emerging from a time when Romanticism was burgeoning across Western Europe, the Grimms sought to preserve oral traditions that reflected the cultural identity of German-speaking peoples. Their work is not only a treasure of narrative art but also a significant artifact from the early 19th century, echoing the era's social values, beliefs, and the quest for a national identity.

The original volume, titled "Kinder- und Hausmärchen" (Children's and Household Tales), first appeared in 1812, featuring tales such as "Hansel and Gretel" and "Snow White." The Grimms meticulously collected these stories from various oral sources and folk traditions, aiming to document and elevate them as part of German literature. Their compilation process was rooted in a desire to safeguard cultural heritage, which they believed was at risk amidst the rapid changes brought about by modernization and industrialization. Over the years, the collection expanded, with subsequent editions adding darker and more complex versions of the tales, reflecting the grim realities of life in the 19th century.

The legacy of Grimms' Fairy Tales is profound, influencing not only literature and popular culture but also shaping the field of folklore studies. Their tales have inspired countless adaptations in literature, theater, and film, while also serving as a vehicle for exploring deeper themes of morality, societal norms, and human psychology. Many stories have become archetypes in Western culture, resonating across generations and transcending geographical boundaries. The Grimms' work laid the foundation for modern children's literature, establishing a framework for the moral and educational purposes of storytelling.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Grimms' Fairy Tales (German: Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 'Children's and Household Tales') is the collection of fairy tales and folk narratives compiled by the brothers Jacob Grimm (1785–1863) and Wilhelm Grimm (1786–1859), first published in two volumes (1812 and 1815) and revised through seven editions (the final edition in 1857) — one of the best-known and most influential works in the Western literary tradition, with the tales translated into over 160 languages and the collection one of the most widely distributed books in history after the Bible. The 1857 edition contains 211 tales, including the most famous fairy tales in the Western canon: Cinderella, Snow White, Rapunzel, Rumpelstiltskin, Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood, Sleeping Beauty, The Frog Prince, and dozens of others.

Grimms' Fairy Tales was presented by the brothers as the rescue of authentic German folk tradition — the collection of oral tales from German peasants and rural storytellers. This claim of authenticity has been substantially revised by subsequent scholarship: many of the tales were contributed by middle-class, often French-influenced informants (including the Hessian storyteller Dorothea Viehmann and the Hassenpflug family), and the tales were heavily edited and revised across editions — with earlier, more violent and sexually explicit versions gradually softened and moralised to suit a family readership. The 'authentic folk tale' was in significant part a literary construction of Romantic nationalism.

The psychological and cultural significance of Grimms' Fairy Tales has been enormous — Bruno Bettelheim's The Uses of Enchantment (1976) argued that fairy tales use archetypal symbolic narratives to help children work through fundamental psychological conflicts, and this psychoanalytic interpretation has shaped a century of scholarship on fairy tales.
